questions.stem: A 43 year old man has had loose, pale, bulky stools and bloating for 8 months, with 5 kg weight loss and tiredness. He drinks 6 units of alcohol a week and has no abdominal pain. He has not travelled. His haemoglobin is 98 g/L with an MCV of 74 fL, and ferritin is low. Colonoscopy was normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chronic steatorrhoea, bloating, weight loss and iron deficiency without alcohol excess or travel is most likely coeliac disease, the commonest mucosal cause of malabsorption.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Steatorrhoea** with **iron deficiency** and weight loss, no pancreatic or travel clue.

elim: Usually gives epigastric pain, with heavy alcohol use.
Follows travel or untreated water; usually weeks, not 8 months.
Does not cause steatorrhoea, weight loss or iron deficiency.

steps.x: **B. Coeliac disease.** Commonest cause of malabsorption: coeliac disease.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with Crohn's disease had 60 cm of terminal ileum resected 6 months ago. Since then she has had watery diarrhoea several times a day and pale, greasy stools. Her Crohn's is in remission on colonoscopy and faecal calprotectin is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her diarrhoea?
questions.e: Bile acids are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum; after resection they reach the colon (diarrhoea) and the bile salt pool falls (fat malabsorption).

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her diarrhoea? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Diarrhoea and steatorrhoea starting after **terminal ileal resection**, Crohn's quiet.

elim: No pancreatic history; pancreatic enzymes are not affected by ileal resection.
Does not explain the timing after ileal resection.
Excluded by normal colonoscopy and calprotectin.
Gives bloating after dairy, not steatorrhoea.

steps.x: **A. Bile acid malabsorption.** Ileal disease or resection: bile salt deficiency and bile acid diarrhoea.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with primary biliary cholangitis has itching, dark urine and jaundice. Her stools have become pale, greasy and difficult to flush. Faecal elastase is normal and coeliac serology is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her steatorrhoea?
o: Reduced bile salt delivery to the gut
questions.e: Cholestatic liver disease reduces bile salt delivery, so micelles cannot form and fat is malabsorbed.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her steatorrhoea? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Cholestasis**, normal pancreas, no coeliac: bile is not reaching the gut.

elim: No blind loop, stricture or dysmotility to suggest it.
Would not explain pale, cholestatic stools.

steps.x: **D. Reduced bile salt delivery to the gut.** Bile salt deficiency (liver or ileal disease) causes fat malabsorption.

questions.stem: A 30 year old aid worker returned from rural India 6 weeks ago. Since then she has had malodorous, non-bloody diarrhoea with flatulence, cramping abdominal pain and 4 kg weight loss. Her stools are greasy. Her temperature is 36.9°C. Coeliac serology is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Weeks of malodorous non-bloody diarrhoea, flatulence and steatorrhoea after travel is giardiasis, an infectious cause of malabsorption.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Travel**, weeks of **non-bloody** malodorous diarrhoea with **steatorrhoea**.

elim: Acute bloody diarrhoea with fever lasting days.

steps.x: **D. Giardia lamblia.** Infectious malabsorption after travel: Giardia lamblia.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man with untreated coeliac disease has noticed easy bruising and bleeding gums. He has steatorrhoea and has lost weight. His platelet count is 260 x10^9/L. Prothrombin time is 19 seconds and APTT is mildly prolonged. He takes no medications.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his bruising?
questions.e: Fat malabsorption causes deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K); low vitamin K reduces clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and prolongs the PT.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his bruising? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Steatorrhoea** plus a **prolonged PT** with normal platelets.

elim: Prolongs APTT only and presents in childhood.
Causes macrocytic anaemia, not a coagulopathy.
Lifelong bleeding with a normal PT.

steps.x: **D. Vitamin K deficiency.** Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins: vitamin K deficiency prolongs PT.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman with coeliac disease has had aching bones and difficulty climbing stairs for 6 months. She has a waddling gait and proximal muscle weakness. Her calcium is 2.02 mmol/L, phosphate 0.6 mmol/L and ALP 260 IU/L. She has struggled to follow a gluten-free diet.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.e: Coeliac villous atrophy reduces absorption of calcium and fat-soluble vitamin D, causing osteomalacia with low calcium and phosphate and raised ALP.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Bone pain, proximal weakness, **low calcium and phosphate**, **raised ALP**: osteomalacia.

elim: Gives fatigue and weight gain, not low calcium and raised ALP.
Calcium, phosphate and ALP are normal in osteoporosis.
Inflammatory shoulder and hip girdle pain in over 50s, with normal bone profile.

steps.x: **E. Vitamin D deficiency.** Malabsorption causes vitamin D and calcium deficiency (osteomalacia).

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has had recurrent epigastric pain radiating to his back for 3 years, worse after meals. He now has bloating and 3 to 4 pale, oily stools a day. He drank heavily for 30 years and recently developed diabetes. Coeliac serology is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent epigastric pain to the back with steatorrhoea and diabetes after long alcohol use is chronic pancreatitis causing pancreatic insufficiency.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Pain to the back, **steatorrhoea**, **diabetes**, alcohol: exocrine and endocrine pancreatic failure.

elim: Serology is negative and it does not cause back-radiating pain.
Gives right iliac fossa pain and non-bloody diarrhoea, not this picture.
Gives biliary colic but not steatorrhoea and diabetes.
Gives epigastric pain but not steatorrhoea.

steps.x: **A. Chronic pancreatitis.** Pancreatic cause of malabsorption: chronic pancreatitis (or cystic fibrosis).

questions.stem: A 22 year old woman has fatigue, bloating, loose stools and recurrent mouth ulcers. Anti-tTG IgA is strongly positive and a duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy. Her doctor checks her blood tests.
questions.q: Which set of results is most likely?
o: High ferritin, high folate and high albumin
High ferritin, low folate and normal albumin
Low ferritin, high folate and high albumin
Low ferritin, low folate and low albumin
Normal ferritin, normal folate and high albumin
questions.e: Coeliac disease affects the proximal small bowel, so iron and folate are malabsorbed, and albumin falls with malabsorption.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which set of results is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Proximal villous atrophy: **iron** and **folate** absorbed in the duodenum and jejunum.

elim: Folate is absorbed proximally and falls in coeliac disease.

steps.x: **D. Low ferritin, low folate and low albumin.** Malabsorption bloods: iron studies, B12, folate, albumin (low).

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with chronic pancreatitis describes his bowel habit. He opens his bowels 3 times a day. He has lost 6 kg in 4 months and feels bloated and tired. He has no rectal bleeding.
questions.q: Which description of his stools is most likely?
o: Pale, bulky and offensive, floating and hard to flush
Small volume with blood and mucus
questions.e: Fat malabsorption causes steatorrhoea: pale, greasy, bulky, foul-smelling stools that float and are difficult to flush, with weight loss and bloating.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which description of his stools is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Chronic pancreatitis** gives fat malabsorption, so expect **steatorrhoea**.

elim: Bile acid diarrhoea, classically after cholecystectomy.

steps.x: **D. Pale, bulky and offensive, floating and hard to flush.** Steatorrhoea: pale, bulky, greasy, offensive, floats.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man has extensive small bowel Crohn's disease affecting the jejunum and ileum. He has never had surgery. He has lost 10 kg and has ankle swelling. His albumin is 24 g/L, B12 is low and ferritin is low. Faecal elastase is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his malabsorption?
o: Bile salt loss after ileal resection
questions.e: Crohn's disease is a mucosal cause of malabsorption: inflamed small bowel absorbs poorly, causing low albumin, iron and B12.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of his malabsorption? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Inflamed **small bowel mucosa**, no surgery, normal pancreas.

elim: Nephrotic syndrome; not explained by Crohn's malabsorption.

steps.x: **C. Mucosal disease reducing absorptive surface.** Mucosal causes of malabsorption: coeliac disease and Crohn's disease.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has had urgent, greenish, watery stools every morning for 8 months. Stool cultures, coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin and colonoscopy with biopsies are normal. She had her gallbladder removed for biliary colic 1 year ago. Her symptoms settle on a trial of a bile acid sequestrant.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Green watery diarrhoea after cholecystectomy that responds to cholestyramine is bile acid malabsorption.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Greenish diarrhoea after **cholecystectomy**, settling on **cholestyramine**.

elim: A diagnosis of exclusion; response to a bile acid sequestrant points to bile acid diarrhoea.

steps.x: **A. Bile acid malabsorption.** Post-cholecystectomy green diarrhoea = bile acid malabsorption; treat with cholestyramine.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has had bloating and loose stools for a year, with mild iron deficiency anaemia. She read online that she might have coeliac disease and stopped eating gluten 2 months ago, which has helped. She would like a test to confirm the diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Diagnose coeliac disease on symptom response
HLA-DQ2 typing as the diagnostic test
Reintroduce gluten for at least 6 weeks before serology
questions.e: Serology (anti-tTG IgA or anti-endomysial antibodies) and biopsy need the patient to be eating gluten; NICE advises gluten in more than one meal a day for at least 6 weeks first.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next step? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
She is **off gluten**, so tests will be falsely negative.

elim: Will be falsely negative while she avoids gluten.
Response to diet is not diagnostic.
Villi may have recovered off gluten, giving a false negative.
A negative result makes coeliac unlikely, but a positive one does not diagnose it.

steps.x: **E. Reintroduce gluten for at least 6 weeks before serology.** Coeliac tests need gluten in the diet (NICE: at least 6 weeks).

questions.stem: A 36 year old man has had fatigue and loose stools for 6 months. His haemoglobin is 112 g/L and ferritin is low. Anti-tTG IgA is strongly positive and anti-endomysial antibodies are positive. He is eating a normal diet.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Duodenal biopsy at upper GI endoscopy
questions.e: Positive serology is followed by duodenal biopsy, the gold standard for coeliac disease, showing villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Serology is **positive**; now the gold-standard confirmation.

elim: Coeliac disease affects the small bowel, not the colon.
Tests bacterial overgrowth or lactose intolerance.

steps.x: **B. Duodenal biopsy at upper GI endoscopy.** Coeliac: anti-tTG IgA first, duodenal biopsy confirms.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man returned from a trekking holiday in Nepal 5 weeks ago, where he drank stream water. He has had foul-smelling, non-bloody diarrhoea, flatulence and bloating since. His temperature is 36.8°C. His haemoglobin and CRP are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Giardiasis is diagnosed with stool microscopy for cysts and trophozoites (stool antigen or PCR also used).

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Travel, **untreated water**, non-bloody diarrhoea with flatulence: **Giardia**.

elim: Tests for coeliac disease; the travel history points to infection.
Used for typhoid, which gives fever.
Invasive; Giardia lives in the small bowel and is found in stool.

steps.x: **E. Stool microscopy.** Giardiasis: stool microscopy.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman has had two admissions with acute pancreatitis. She now has 4 months of bloating and pale, greasy stools that are hard to flush. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Coeliac serology is negative and her HbA1c is 52 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to assess the cause of her steatorrhoea?
questions.e: Faecal elastase assesses pancreatic exocrine insufficiency in suspected chronic pancreatitis (NICE chronic pancreatitis guidance); a low result supports a pancreatic cause.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to assess the cause of her steatorrhoea? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Recurrent pancreatitis, **steatorrhoea** and new **diabetes**: is the pancreas failing?

elim: Rises in acute attacks but does not measure exocrine reserve.

steps.x: **C. Faecal elastase.** Pancreatic insufficiency: faecal elastase (low).

questions.stem: A 57 year old man describes 3 months of pale, offensive stools that float and are difficult to flush. His GP wants to confirm objectively that he has steatorrhoea before further tests. He has lost 3 kg.
questions.q: Which stool test is most appropriate?
o: Stool microscopy for ova and parasites
questions.e: Faecal fat measurement confirms steatorrhoea; specific tests then look for the cause.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which stool test is most appropriate? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: confirm objectively that he has steatorrhoea
steps.x: The question is whether there is **fat** in the stool.

elim: Detects blood for colorectal cancer screening.

steps.x: **B. Faecal fat measurement.** Steatorrhoea is confirmed with faecal fat.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has had diarrhoea, bloating and 7 kg weight loss for 6 months. She looks pale and has angular stomatitis and ankle oedema. Her GP suspects malabsorption and wants to assess her nutritional state before referral.
questions.q: Which set of blood tests is most appropriate?
o: Full blood count, iron studies, B12, folate and albumin
questions.e: In malabsorption, blood tests look for deficiencies: FBC, iron studies, B12, folate and albumin (low), and these are repeated to monitor response.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which set of blood tests is most appropriate? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Pallor, angular stomatitis, **oedema**: look for **iron, B12, folate and albumin** deficits.

elim: Mark acute pancreatitis, not nutritional state.

steps.x: **C. Full blood count, iron studies, B12, folate and albumin.** Malabsorption bloods: iron, B12, folate, albumin.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has had 9 months of diarrhoea, steatorrhoea and weight loss. Anti-tTG IgA (with normal total IgA), stool microscopy, faecal elastase and colonoscopy are all normal. He has not travelled and does not drink alcohol.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Upper GI endoscopy with small bowel biopsies
questions.e: When first-line tests do not explain malabsorption, endoscopy with biopsy is used to find a specific cause.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
First-line tests have **not found the cause** of persistent malabsorption.

elim: Does not identify a mucosal cause.
Already normal with normal total IgA.

steps.x: **E. Upper GI endoscopy with small bowel biopsies.** Unclear malabsorption: endoscopy with biopsy.

questions.stem: A 6 year old girl has had foul-smelling diarrhoea, bloating and abdominal pain for 3 weeks. Several children at her nursery have similar symptoms. Stool microscopy shows Giardia lamblia cysts. She is drinking well and is afebrile.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Giardiasis is treated first line with oral metronidazole.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Confirmed **Giardia** in a child.

elim: Giardiasis should be treated to clear infection and limit spread.

steps.x: **D. Oral metronidazole.** Giardiasis: oral metronidazole.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man with alcohol-related chronic pancreatitis has steatorrhoea and has lost 8 kg. Faecal elastase is very low. He has stopped drinking. He asks if anything can help his stools and weight.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Pancreatic insufficiency is treated by replacing the missing enzymes (Creon) with meals and snacks, treating the underlying cause of malabsorption.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency** confirmed.

elim: Treats the symptom, not the missing enzymes.

steps.x: **E. Pancreatic enzyme replacement with meals.** Pancreatic malabsorption: pancreatic enzyme replacement (Creon).

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with Crohn's disease had a terminal ileal resection 4 months ago. Since then she has had urgent watery diarrhoea 5 times a day. Colonoscopy shows no active Crohn's and a SeHCAT scan shows reduced bile acid retention.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Bile acid malabsorption after ileal resection is treated with cholestyramine, which binds bile acids in the gut.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Bile acid malabsorption **confirmed** after ileal resection.

elim: Pancreatic function is not the problem.

steps.x: **A. Cholestyramine.** Bile acid malabsorption: cholestyramine.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man with biopsy-proven coeliac disease started a gluten-free diet 12 months ago. He still has bloating and loose stools, and his anti-tTG IgA remains raised. He eats out several times a week and drinks beer at weekends.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Dietitian review of hidden gluten intake
Reintroduce gluten as the diet has failed
questions.e: The treatment for coeliac disease is a lifelong gluten-free diet; persistent symptoms and raised tTG usually mean ongoing gluten exposure (beer, eating out), so a dietitian review is next.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Raised tTG means he is still **eating gluten** (beer, eating out).

elim: For refractory coeliac disease only after excluding gluten exposure.
Not first line; ongoing gluten is the likely cause.
Not indicated without evidence of pancreatic insufficiency.
The diet is lifelong; it has not failed if gluten is still eaten.

steps.x: **A. Dietitian review of hidden gluten intake.** Coeliac disease: lifelong strict gluten-free diet; raised tTG means gluten exposure.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman with coeliac disease has started a gluten-free diet. She has iron deficiency anaemia, low folate and a low vitamin D level. Her weight has fallen by 6 kg over the past year.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional long-term management?
o: No further action once on the diet
Supplements with monitoring of weight and repeat bloods
questions.e: Malabsorption is managed long term with nutritional support, vitamin and mineral supplements, and monitoring of weight and repeat bloods.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate additional long-term management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Several **deficiencies** and weight loss despite treating the cause.

elim: Not needed for stable iron deficiency.
For intestinal failure, not coeliac disease.

steps.x: **D. Supplements with monitoring of weight and repeat bloods.** Long term: supplements, weight monitoring, repeat bloods.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has steatorrhoea, bloating and weight loss for 6 weeks after returning from Peru. Stool microscopy shows Giardia cysts. He is also found to have low folate. He asks whether he needs a gluten-free diet as his friend with similar symptoms does.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Supportive fluids and review in 6 months
Treat the infection and correct the deficiency
questions.e: Malabsorption is treated by treating its specific cause (here metronidazole for Giardia) plus nutritional support for deficiencies.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
The **cause** is Giardia, and there is a **deficiency**.

elim: For coeliac disease, which has not been diagnosed.

steps.x: **E. Treat the infection and correct the deficiency.** Treat the underlying cause, and replace what is missing.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman with coeliac disease asks what in her diet causes the damage to her bowel. Her duodenal biopsy showed villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytes.
questions.q: Which dietary component most likely triggers the immune response?
questions.e: Coeliac disease is an autoimmune reaction to gluten, specifically gliadin, causing villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia in the proximal small bowel.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which dietary component most likely triggers the immune response? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Coeliac disease is a reaction to **gluten**; which part?

elim: A milk protein; relevant to cow's milk protein allergy.
Can cause osmotic diarrhoea in fructose malabsorption.
Causes symptoms in lactase deficiency, not autoimmune villous atrophy.
Fat is malabsorbed in coeliac disease but does not trigger it.

steps.x: **C. Gliadin.** Coeliac disease: autoimmune reaction to gliadin in gluten.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man with cystic fibrosis has bulky, offensive stools that float. His faecal elastase is very low. His duodenal biopsy, taken for another reason, shows normal villi.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his steatorrhoea?
o: Failure of fat digestion from low lipase
Giardia adherence to the brush border
questions.e: Pancreatic insufficiency reduces secretion of lipase, amylase and protease, so fat is not digested (not just not absorbed), causing steatorrhoea.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of his steatorrhoea? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Pancreas failing, mucosa **normal**: the problem is **digestion**.

elim: Bile acid malabsorption, not CF pancreatic disease.
Villi are normal, so absorption is intact.

steps.x: **B. Failure of fat digestion from low lipase.** Pancreatic steatorrhoea: low lipase impairs fat digestion.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman had an extensive terminal ileal resection for Crohn's disease. She now has steatorrhoea, night blindness and a prolonged prothrombin time. Her pancreatic function is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her vitamin deficiencies?
o: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells
Bacterial consumption of vitamins in the colon
Impaired micelle formation from loss of bile acids
questions.e: Bile acids are needed for micelle formation; without them fat and fat-soluble vitamins (A for night vision, K for clotting) are malabsorbed.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of her vitamin deficiencies? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Deficiency of **vitamins A and K**, both fat-soluble, after **ileal** loss.

elim: Pernicious anaemia, causing B12 deficiency only.

steps.x: **C. Impaired micelle formation from loss of bile acids.** Bile acids form micelles that carry fat and fat-soluble vitamins.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has watery diarrhoea since a cholecystectomy 9 months ago. A SeHCAT scan confirms bile acid malabsorption. She asks why losing bile acids gives her watery diarrhoea.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her diarrhoea?
o: Autoimmune damage to small bowel villi
Unabsorbed bile acids irritating the colon
questions.e: Unabsorbed bile acids reaching the colon irritate it and stimulate secretion, causing watery diarrhoea, alongside fat malabsorption.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of her diarrhoea? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Bile acids reaching the **colon** in excess.
**E. Unabsorbed bile acids irritating the colon.** Bile acid diarrhoea: colonic irritation by unabsorbed bile acids.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has 4 weeks of non-bloody, greasy diarrhoea after drinking well water on holiday. Duodenal biopsy shows pear-shaped organisms attached to the surface epithelium with no tissue invasion. Faecal calprotectin is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the absence of blood in his stool?
o: The organism adheres to the brush border without invading
The organism invades through M cells
The organism lives only in the colon
The organism produces a preformed toxin
questions.e: Giardia lamblia attaches to the duodenal and jejunal mucosa, disrupting the brush border mechanically or by toxins without invading, so diarrhoea is non-bloody with malabsorption.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely explanation for the absence of blood in his stool? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Organisms sit **on** the surface and do **not invade**.

elim: Giardia lives in the duodenum and jejunum.

steps.x: **A. The organism adheres to the brush border without invading.** Giardia: brush border disruption without invasion, so no blood.
